title: Transformative Constitutionalism
lead: The idea that a Constitution is ==not a static legal document but a dynamic instrument== meant to transform society by dismantling entrenched inequalities and hierarchies. Coined in ==South African constitutional discourse==, it gained prominence in Indian jurisprudence ==post-2010s== — the Constitution as a ==living document==.

head: Provision
Transformative implication
rows: Establishes ==justice, liberty, equality and fraternity== as core values aimed at transforming Indian society.
Empowers citizens and restrains state power — abolishes ==untouchability (Art 17)==, guarantees ==equality (14)==, ==freedom (19)==, ==life with dignity (21)==.
Articulates socio-economic goals — ==education, health, living wage== — directing the State toward justice and welfare.
Judicial review and constitutional remedies ensure ==enforcement of rights and corrective interpretation==.

items.title: Social Transformation
bullets: ==Art 17== abolished untouchability
[[Sabarimala (2018)]]: exclusion of women based on menstruation violates ==Arts 14, 15 and 25==
[[Navtej Singh Johar (2018)]]: decriminalised homosexuality — ==dignity and identity of LGBTQ+ persons==

items.title: Caste & Reservation
bullets: [[Indra Sawhney (1992)]]: upheld OBC reservations with the ==creamy layer==
[[Jarnail Singh (2018)]]: creamy layer extended to ==SC/ST promotions==
[[State of Punjab v. Davinder Singh (2024)]]: states may ==sub-categorise==

items.title: Gender Justice
bullets: [[Vishaka (1997)]]: guidelines using ==international conventions== absent domestic law
[[Joseph Shine (2018)]]: decriminalised adultery as ==discriminatory against women==

items.title: Environmental Justice
bullets: ==M.C. Mehta cases==: ==polluter pays==, environmental impact assessments, and the ==right to clean air and water== read into Art 21

items.title: Economic & Labour Rights
bullets: [[Olga Tellis (1985)]]: ==right to livelihood== intrinsic to Art 21
[[Workmen v. Meenakshi Mills (1992)]]: fair treatment and ==collective bargaining==
[[PUCL v. UoI (2001 onwards)]]: ==right to food==, leading to MGNREGA and midday meals

items.title: Emerging & Intersectional Rights
bullets: [[K.S. Puttaswamy (2017)]]: ==privacy as intrinsic to Art 21==
Foundation for ==data protection, bodily autonomy, sexual identity rights==

head: Phase
Judicial approach
Example
rows: Puttaswamy, Navtej Johar, Sabarimala, Joseph Shine

items: ==Majoritarianism vs minority rights== — communal rhetoric and laws (anti-conversion laws) challenge secular, egalitarian aims; the ==CAA (2019)== criticised for violating Art 14.
==Executive resistance and underenforcement== — judgments not effectively implemented (==manual scavenging persists== despite Art 17 and court orders); Centre–state disputes over welfare schemes.
==Patriarchal social structures== — societal norms restrict actual transformation (==opposition to the Sabarimala verdict==).
==Judicial overreach vs restraint== — critics argue courts exceed constitutional limits in pursuit of social justice, undermining democratic accountability.
==Access to justice== — structural inequalities, low legal awareness and delays impede realisation for the marginalised.

items.title: Case Studies
bullets: [[Navtej Singh Johar (2018)]] — transformative on LGBTQ+ rights; grounded in ==dignity, privacy, autonomy==
[[S.R. Bommai (1994)]] — ==secularism as basic structure==; limited misuse of Art 356, strengthening federalism
[[NALSA v. UoI (2014)]] — recognised transgender persons as the ==‘third gender’==; directed reservations, education and legal protection

items.title: Policy Translation
bullets: ==Education==: ==RTE Act (2009)== under Art 21A — enhanced enrolment of disadvantaged children
==Health==: Ayushman Bharat, Janani Suraksha Yojana
==Food security==: ==National Food Security Act (2013)== — built on judicial recognition of the right to food
==Gender rights==: One Stop Centres, ==POSH Act==

blocks.text: Transformative constitutionalism in India is not a destination but a continuous journey. While courts have played a pivotal role in expanding rights, real transformation requires a concerted effort from the legislature, executive and civil society to implement these ideals on the ground.
